title: Design of catalyst for syngas conversion to C2 oxygenates via confining diatomic metal within the framework of 2D carbon-based materials
abstract: The selectivity of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates still faces a big challenge. In the present study, the different 2D carbon-based substrates (g-C3N4, GDY and C2N) supported diatomic RhCo catalysts are constructed reasonably to enhance C2 oxygenates selectivity. The complicated reaction network is studied by means of DFT calculations; the influences of the species coverage, the reaction temperature and pressure are examined using microkinetic modeling. The results indicate that RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts have excellent structural stability. The preferred existence form of CHx(x = 1–3) monomer, as well as the activity and selectivity of CHx monomer and C2 oxygenates generation are strongly related to the coordination environment of 2D carbon-based material supported diatomic RhCo catalysts. The screened RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst could perform the outstanding catalytic performance toward the generation of C2 oxygenates CH2CO and CH3CO, in which the coordination environment of g-C3N4 makes the diatomic RhCo cluster lose more electron and d-band center far away from Fermi level. This work provides an alternative way to construct 2D substrate supported diatomic metal catalysts in syngas-to-C2 oxygenates, adjusting 2D substrate type could change the local coordination environment of diatomic metal sites and further improve catalytic performance.
paragraphs: Synthesis of C2 oxygenates through syngas (CO + H2) transformation is an important way for converting biomass, carbon dioxide, natural gas, and coal into the valuable chemicals [1], [2], [3], [4], but the low C2 oxygenates selectivity and yield remain challenging. At present, the diatomic metal catalysts [5], [6] could perform nearly 100 % atomic utilization efficiency, compared with the single-atom catalyst, it provides the multiple active sites, and the synergism effect between two metal atoms exhibits high catalytic performance toward CO hydrogenation, CO oxidation, CO2 hydrogenation and nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR) [7], [8].

In the diatomic metal catalysts, the surface free energy of metal atom is relatively high, which easily results in the production of small clusters due to the migration and aggregation of metal atom, and the catalytic performance greatly decreases [9]. Thus, the suitable substrate is greatly significant to stabilize the metal active sites [10], [11]. In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) carbon-based materials, such as graphdiyne (GDY), porous graphene nitride (C2N) and graphite-phase carbon nitride (g-C3N4), are generally applied as the substrate to stably anchor the metal atoms due to their unique pore structure, coordination environment and electronic properties [12], [13], [14]. For example, Qian et al. [15] theoretically showed that C2N acted as the substrate could stabilize diatomic Cr2 and V2 active sites in the diatomic Cr2/C2N and V2/C2N catalysts to exhibit great thermal stability during the process of NRR. Zhao et al. [16] found that the strong interaction between Cu2 and C2N substrate in the diatomic Cu2/C2N catalyst ensured the stability of Cu2 active site and performed high catalytic activity toward the electrochemical reduction of CO2 to hydrocarbons. Yang et al. [17] suggested that g-C3N4 substrate exhibited the unique coordination environment to make the diatomic Cu with nearly +1 charge in the diatomic Cu2/g-C3N4 catalyst, which exhibited excellent catalytic performance for the oxidation of CH4 to C1 oxygenates. Li et al. [18] found that C2N substrate altered d-band center of FeCu active site in the diatomic FeCu/C2N catalyst, which improved the adsorption strength of key intermediates in CO oxidation to present high activity. Ding et al. [19] experimentally and theoretically confirmed that g-C3N4 could provide favorable coordination environment for CO2 transformation to CO over the diatomic NiCu/g-C3N4 and NiMn/g-C3N4 catalysts, moreover, the synergistic effect between Ni and Cu/Mn atoms greatly enhanced catalytic activity. Thus, the GDY, C2N and g-C3N4 acted as the substrate could greatly stabilize the diatomic metals, and the synergistic effect between two metal atoms could improve catalytic performance.

On the other hand, the previously reported studies indicated that C2 oxygenate generation from syngas primarily undergoes two key steps [20], [21], [22]: the first step is CO activation to generate CHx intermediate via two main paths: (1) C atom from CO direct dissociation is hydrogenated to generate CHx; (2) CO hydrogenation generates the intermediates CHxOH (x = 1,2) and CHxO (x = 1–3), then, CHx is generated via their CO bond cleavage; meanwhile, CH3OH can be also generated by the hydrogenation of CHxOH (x = 1,2) and CHxO(x = 1–3) to decrease CHx selectivity. The second step is CO/CHO reacting with CHx to generate C2 oxygenates, meanwhile, the occurrence of CHx hydrogenation or coupling to generate by-product methane or C2 hydrocarbons, leading to the decrease of C2 oxygenates selectivity. Aiming at realizing the high activity and selectivity of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates, it is necessary to efficiently promote CO activation to generate CHx and achieve the CC bond formation, as well as inhibits the formation of by-products such as methane, methanol and C2 hydrocarbons.

Nowadays, the experimental and theoretical studies showed that the metal Rh has high C2 oxygenates selectivity in syngas conversion due to the unique CO adsorption and activation ability, however, it presents low CO conversion and facilitates the generation of by-product methane [23], [24]. The metal Co has excellent CO dissociation ability to produce CHx and facilitates carbon-chain formation in the FTS reaction, however, the main product is C2+ hydrocarbon [25], [26]. Remarkably, the combination of Rh and Co to form RhCo bimetallic catalyst may perform great catalytic performance for CO activation and C2 oxygenates generation in syngas conversion. For example, Zhong et al. [27] found that the bimetallic RhCo active site could adjust CO adsorption intensity and perform excellent catalytic performance toward the transformation of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates over the bimetallic RhCo catalyst. Xie et al. [28] showed that the bimetallic RhCo/OCNT catalyst exhibited higher CO conversion (53.0 %) compared to the single metal Rh/OCNT catalyst (24.8 %), in which Rh and Co atoms present the synergistic effect. Inspired by above studies, it is proposed that whether the diatomic RhCo active sites anchored over the carbon-based materials such as GDY, C2N and g-C3N4 could present high catalytic performance induced by the synergistic effect between Rh and Co, and exhibit excellent stability during C2 oxygenate synthesis from syngas? Moreover, until now, few investigations about syngas transformation to C2 oxygenates have been reported over the carbon-based substrate supported diatomic RhCo catalysts; further, the influences of coordination environment of carbon-based substrate and the synergistic effect between Rh and Co on the catalytic performance of C2 oxygenates are also unclear.

In this study, an integrated method by combining DFT calculations with microkinetic modeling is carried out to discuss the detailed reaction mechanism for the transformation of syngas to C2 oxygenates over different carbon-based substrates supported diatomic RhCo catalysts. Here, three types of g-C3N4, GDY and C2N substrates are employed to present different coordination environment of diatomic RhCo active site; the roles of coordination environment in the diatomic RhCo catalysts and synergistic effect between Rh and Co in regulating catalytic performance toward the transformation of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates are expected to be identified. Furthermore, the electronic properties are examined aiming at revealing microscopic essence of coordination environment in regulating catalytic performance and provide a theoretical basis for designing and optimizing diatomic metal catalysts to present better catalytic performance by adjusting the types of carbon-based substrate.

All DFT calculations were completed in the Dmol3 code of Materials Studio 8.0 package [29], [30] To describe the exchange–correlation functional, the generalized gradient approximation (GGA-PBE) is employed [31], [32]. Metal atoms and non-metal atoms adopt effective core potential (ECP) and all-electron basis sets, respectively [33]. The double-numerical plus polarization (DNP) was employed to expand the valence electron wave function [34], [35]. The displacement, force and energy accuracy correspond to the convergence criteria of 5 × 10−3 Å, 1 × 10−3 Ha/Å and 1 × 10−5 Ha, respectively. A 3 × 3 × 1 k-point grids was adopted. The smearing value of 0.005 Hartree was used. Van der Waals interaction has been considered [36]. The complete linear synchronous transit/quadratic synchronous transit (LST/QST) method was employed to search transition state [37], [38]. TS Confirmation and Vibrational Analysis methods were carried out to ensure the rationality of transition states.

The thermal stability of diatomic catalyst are examined by utilizing the method of Ab initio molecular dynamics simulation (AIMD) [39]. NVT ensemble conducted for AIMD simulations at a time step of 1 fs was performed for 10 ps. In the simulation process, the temperature was controlled by Nose-Hoover thermostat method [40], only the gamma points of Brillouin zone was selected, and the symmetry of diatomic catalyst is not restricted.

Based on the previously experimental [41] and theoretical [42], [43], [44] studies, three types of RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are constructed, firstly, the single-layer g-C3N4, GDY and C2N with p(2 × 2) supercell are constructed; then putting the diatomic RhCo cluster into the hole center of the substrate. To ignore the interaction between the periodic layer and the layer, the thickness of the vacuum layer is set to 15 Å. Meanwhile, the optimized stable configurations of RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are presented in Fig. 1a, in which Rh atom is anchored with four C atoms; Co atom is anchored with five C atoms over RhCo/GDY. Similarly, Wang et al. [45] constructed the model of diatomic Pd1Ag1/GDY and Pd1Ni1/GDY catalysts, in which Pd atom is also anchored with four C atoms; Ag or Ni atom is anchored with five C atoms. For RhCo/g-C3N4, both Rh and Co atoms are coordinated with two pyridine-N atoms, and the Rh/Co, N and C atoms form a six-membered ring. Previous studies [46] also showed that Fe atom was anchored with two pyridine-N atoms, and the Fe, N and C atoms form a six-membered ring in the diatomic Fe/g-C3N4. For RhCo/C2N, both Rh and Co atoms are coordinated with two pyridine-N atoms; the Rh/Co, N and C atoms form a five-membered ring. Li et al. [18] build the models of diatomic M2/C2N (M = Pt, Co, Ni and Cu) catalysts, in which Pt, Co, Ni or Cu atom are all coordinated with two pyridine-N atoms, and the Pt/Co/Ni/Cu, N and C atoms form a five-membered ring. Over FeCo/C2N [43], the Fe or Co atom is coordinated with two pyridine-N atoms, and the Fe/Co, N and C atoms form a five-membered ring. Moreover, the bond lengths of Co − N are 1.833 and 1.842 Å in RhCo/g-C3N4, which is less than that in RhCo/C2N (1.901 and 2.055 Å). The bond lengths of Rh − N are 1.954 and 1.990 Å in RhCo/g-C3N4, while these are 2.053 and 1.953 Å in RhCo/C2N. Thus, the different substrates result in different coordination environment of diatomic RhCo cluster in RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts.

The structural stability of RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts is evaluated by the energy difference (Eaverage BE-Eaverage coh) between the average binding energy (Eaverage BE) of RhCo and the average cohesive energy (Eaverage coh) of Rh and Co in the bulk [47], [48]. According to this definition, the more negative value corresponds to the higher catalyst stability, suggesting that the occurrence of metal atom migration or aggregation to form small metal cluster is difficult. Meanwhile, the average binding energy and the average cohesive energy can be obtained by the following equation [49]:Eaverage BE=(ERhCo-sub-Esub-ERh atom-ECo atom)/2.Eaverage coh=(Ecoh-Rh + Ecoh-Co)/2.where ERhCo-sub, ERh atom, ECo atom and Esub represent the total energies of the diatomic RhCo catalysts, the single-atom Rh, Co and carbon-based substrates, respectively. Ecoh-Rh and Ecoh-Co correspond to the cohesive energies of the bulk Rh and Co obtained by Kittel et al. [50], respectively.

As listed in Table S1, the Eaverage BE of RhCo in the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are −9.40, −11.03 and −11.43 eV, respectively. The energy released by the aggregation of single-atom Rh/Co to form bulk metal Rh/Co is 5.75/4.39 eV/atom, respectively; correspondingly, the values of ECoh-Rh and ECoh-Co are −5.75 and −4.39 eV [50]. Thus, the Eaverage coh is −5.07 eV. Further, as shown in Fig. 1a, the energy difference (Eaverage BE-Eaverage coh) between the average binding energy (Eaverage BE) of RhCo and the average cohesive energy (Eaverage coh) are −4.33, −5.96 and −6.36 eV over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N, respectively. Above result shows that three types of diatomic RhCo catalysts have high structural stability. Compared with g-C3N4 substrate, both GDY and C2N substrates provide better structural stability, which is attributed to that the coordination environment of GDY and C2N substrates is more conducive to anchor RhCo, namely, the structural stability of diatomic RhCo catalysts is closely linked with the coordination environment of the substrate.

The essentially determined factor to affect the structural stability of diatomic RhCo catalysts is studied by analyzing their electronic properties such as the differential charge density and average Bader charge. The differential charge density of RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts (see Fig. 1b) indicates that the local charge distribution greatly depends on the type of carbon-based substrates, in which the obvious electron transfer occurs between the metal atoms and the substrate. More specifically, g-C3N4 substrate accepts the electrons, RhCo cluster lose the electrons in RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst; however, in the RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts, the GDY and C2N substrates lose the electrons, RhCo cluster accepts the electrons. To quantitatively analyze the electron number of RhCo cluster, the average Bader charge is calculated. The average Bader charge of RhCo cluster over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are −0.49, 2.70 and 2.46 e, respectively, suggesting that the more electron transfer between GDY/C2N substrate and RhCo cluster compared with that between g-C3N4 substrate and RhCo cluster, namely, the stronger interaction between GDY/C2N substrate and RhCo cluster results in highly structural stability. Thus, it is concluded that the coordination environment of anchored substrate alters the electronic properties of RhCo cluster leading to different structural stability of diatomic RhCo catalysts.

Furthermore, the catalyst stability is also greatly impacted by the electronic properties over the other 2D carbon-based substrate supported metal catalysts. For example, Liu et al. [51] found that Fe/GDY has high stability, which is attributed to the occurrence of charge transfer from Fe atom to GDY, resulting in strong interaction between Fe and GDY. Bader charge analysis shows that the greater electrons transfer from Pd atom to α-MoC in Pd1/α-MoC catalyst compared with the Pdn/α-MoC (n = 2–7) catalysts, which means that Pd single atoms can be greatly stabilized on α-MoC surface and performs the excellent stability [52]. An increased electron transfer from Pt atom to support occurs in Pt1/N-doped graphene compared with that in Pt2/N-doped graphene, which results in the higher stability of Pt1/N-doped graphene [53].

Since syngas transformation to generate C2 oxygenates over Rh-based catalysts usually occurs at temperature range from 500 K to 623 K [54], [55], 525 K is mainly considered in this study. The complicated reaction network involving in the transformation of syngas to C2 oxygenates over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are mapped out in Fig. 2. Meanwhile, Table 1 lists the calculated reaction free energy and activation free energy of each elementary step.

For CO initial activation, H-assisted activation of CO bond and its direct decomposition to C and O have been considered. Over RhCo/g-C3N4, see Fig. 3a, CHO generation requires activation free energy of 115.0 kJ·mol−1, the corresponding reaction free energy is 36.9 kJ·mol−1, which is considered as the preferable path for CO activation compared to COH generation and CO direct dissociation in kinetics (384.6 and 323.6 kJ·mol−1) and thermodynamics (113.8 and 248.9 kJ·mol−1). As shown in Fig. 3b and 3c, the same thing also occurs over RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts. Namely, CHO generation is the most preferred path for CO activation thermodynamically and kinetically compared to COH generation and CO direct dissociation, CO activation ability follows the order of RhCo/g-C3N4 > RhCo/GDY > RhCo/C2N (115.0, 149.2 and 250.6 kJ·mol−1), suggesting that the type of carbon-based substrate in the diatomic RhCo catalysts affects the activity of CO initial activation arisen from different coordination environment of RhCo active sites.

During the process of CO hydrogenation, a vital step for supplying hydrogen source is the adsorption and dissociation of H2, thus, it was firstly examined over the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts. As presented in Fig. S2, H2 dissociative adsorption easily occurs to produce adsorbed H atoms over the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts. Namely, the dissociation of H2 into H atom over the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts is spontaneous, which can offer abundant hydrogen source to participate into the hydrogenation reaction. Meanwhile, H2 dissociation is not the rate-controlled step in syngas transformation to C2 oxygenates, which does not impact the activity of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates over the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts.
For CH generation, as shown in Fig. 2, two possible paths via the CO bond scission of CHO or CHOH intermediate (Paths 1–1 and 1–2) are considered.

For CH2 generation, see Fig. 2, four possible generation paths (Paths 2–1 ∼ 2–4) are examined, including the direct CO bond scission of CH2O/CH2OH, and CH served as precursor is hydrogenated to generate CH2.
For CH3 generation, five paths (Paths 3–1 ∼ 3–5) via the CO bond scission in CH3O intermediate, and the hydrogenation of CH/CH2 served as precursor from different paths are considered.
For CH3OH generation, as illustrated in Fig. 2, three paths (Paths 4–1 ∼ 4–3) via the hydrogenation of CH3O or CH2OH are considered.

Beginning with CO + H species, the corresponding overall barriers of the most preferred paths for CHx(x = 1–3) and CH3OH generation over three diatomic RhCo catalysts are shown in Fig. 5, CH2 and CH3 are easily generated in kinetics compared to CH generation over RhCo/g-C3N4 (116.9, 116.9 vs 262.7 kJ·mol−1), RhCo/GDY (237.7, 237.7 vs 364.6 kJ·mol−1) and RhCo/C2N (320.0, 320.0 vs 323.6 kJ·mol−1). Moreover, as obtained in Section 3.4.4, CH3 primarily comes from CH2 hydrogenation, suggesting that CH2 could be served as the precursor to generate CH3, correspondingly, the most abundant CHx monomer should be CH2 species.

For CH2 generation, as shown in Fig. 4, Path 2–2 is the preferred path on RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst; Path 2–3 is dominant over RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts. For methanol, Path 4–2 is preferred over RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst, that is Path 4–1 over RhCo/C2N, and it is Path 4–3 over RhCo/GDY. Thus, the coordination environment alters the most preferred generation path of CH2 monomer and methanol, which may greatly impact their activity and selectivity.

Considering the influences of the operating temperature, pressure, and species coverage on the transformation of syngas-to-CHx(x = 1–3) at the experimental conditions (PH2 = 8 atm, PCO = 4 atm; T = 525 K). The microkinetic modeling (see details in the Supplementary Material) is carried out to further understand the role of coordination environment in regulating the catalytic performance of syngas transformation to CHx(x = 1–3) over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts.

As displayed in Fig. 5b, the results based on microkinetic modeling demonstrate that RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY catalysts presents the higher generation rate of CH2/CH3 compared to that of CH, which is in good agreement with DFT result. However, over RhCo/C2N, the generation rate of CH is higher than that of CH2/CH3, which is not consistent with DFT result; namely, the generation rate of CHx(x = 1–3) is affected by the activation free energy, moreover, it is also determined by the species coverage. Previous studies also showed that the species coverage greatly impacts the activity and selectivity of product [56], [57], [58]. For example, Yao et al. [57] compared the TOF based on the non-coverage-dependent and coverage-dependent kinetic mode, in which TOF based on the coverage-dependent kinetic model is approximately 6 orders of magnitude larger than that based on the non-coverage-dependent kinetic model, namely, the activity and selectivity of product is closely linked with the species coverage. DFT calculations by Braga et al. [58] found that the activation barrier of alkane combining with metallocarbene (alkane activation) is higher than that of diazo molecule combining with metallocarbene (dimerization reaction), which does not agree with the experimental results that alkane activation is more feasible, this situation is attributed to that the high coverage of alkane is not considered, leading to the higher rate of alkane activation compared to the dimerization reaction. Thus, the obtained results have the difference between the microkinetic modelling and DFT calculations [59]. The generation rate (molecules·s−1·site−1) of preferred CHx(x = 1–3) monomer is RhCo/g-C3N4 (1.60 × 10−18) > RhCo/GDY (2.83 × 10−22) > RhCo/C2N (1.03 × 10−42), suggesting that the g-C3N4 substrate provides the preferred coordination environment to increase the generation rate of CHx monomer. The generation rate of methanol is RhCo/GDY (2.16 × 10−28) > RhCo/C2N (1.21 × 10−28) > RhCo/g-C3N4 (1.91 × 10−34), indicating that g-C3N4 substrate provides the preferred coordination environment to decrease the rate of methanol generation.

Above analysis suggested that the activity of the preferred CHx(x = 1–3) monomer and methanol generation is greatly impacted by the coordination environment, which is well supported by previously reported literatures. For instance, DFT studies by Wang et al. [60] found that Co/N-doped graphene catalyst performed higher activity of oxygen reduction reaction compared to Co/C2N, Co/C3N4 and Co/graphene catalysts. Liu et al. [61] showed that W/N-doped graphene reaches the lower limiting potentials for NRR compared with W/C2N. Hunter et al. [62] found that N8V4 substrate provides more favorable coordination environment for diatomic CoPt active site to perform excellent activity of ORR in comparison with N6V4 substrate.

Methanol is an unwanted product during the transformation process of syngas to CHx(x = 1–3) leading to the reduced CHx selectivity. As depicted in Fig. 5b, based on microkinetic modeling, RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts correspond to methanol selectivity of 0 %, 0 % and 100 %, respectively (see Table S4). CH3 selectivity is 82.7 %, 81.6 % and 0 %, respectively; CH2 selectivity is 17.3 %, 18.4 % and 0 %, respectively, suggesting that the coordination environment could obviously affect the selectivity of the preferred CHx monomer. Thus, among these three RhCo catalysts, methanol generation is unfavored on RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY catalysts, which tends to supply the abundant CHx monomer to facilitate C2 oxygenates generation.

Furthermore, the previously reported studies also showed that the coordination environment plays a vital role in tuning catalytic performance over the 2D carbon-based substrate supported metal catalysts [63], [64], [65], [66]. For example, DFT studies by Wu et al. [63] constructed the different Fe/graphene with single vacancy catalysts (Fe/SV-Gr), in which C atoms around the vacancy were replaced by one, two or three N atoms (denoted as FeN1/SV-Gr, FeN2/SV-Gr and FeN3/SV-Gr) to alter the coordination environment of Fe, the results showed that FeN3/SV-Gr performed higher ability toward CH bond breaking of CH4 compared with the other catalysts, suggesting that the coordination environment plays a significant role in tuning catalytic performance. Zhou et al. [64] also found that the coordination environment of Pt greatly impacted the activity and selectivity toward ethylene production during the process of C2H2 semi-hydrogenation over the Pt1/SV-graphene and Pt1/DV-graphene catalysts. Zhao et al. [66] fully investigated that the effect of coordination environment on catalytic performance of CO2 reduction to CO over the Ni1Nx/DV-graphene (x = 0–4) catalysts, suggesting that the Ni1N/DV-graphene and Ni1N3/DV-graphene catalysts have outstanding activity and selectivity toward CO production.

The catalytic performance of carbon-based material supported diatomic catalysts is essentially determined by their electronic structure, moreover, the electronic properties of diatomic metal active sites could be altered by substrate type to affect their catalytic performance [67], [68]. Thus, it is necessary to clarify the intrinsic reason to determine the catalytic performance by analyzing electronic properties.

The average Bader charges of RhCo atoms over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts are −0.49, 2.70 and 2.46 e, respectively. Over RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts, as display in Fig. S7, RhCo cluster has the d-band center of −3.22, −2.37 and −2.98 eV, respectively. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 6, the relationship of the average Bader charge and d-band center with CH2 generation activity over the diatomic RhCo catalysts presents the volcanic-type curve. Specifically, g-C3N4 substrate results in RhCo active sites with the greater number of loss electrons and the greater downshifted d-band center, which exhibit the highest activity.

Importantly, the adsorption ability of key intermediate is impacted by their electronic properties such as d-band center and Bader charge [69], [70], resulting in the change of catalytic performance. For example, FeN4/graphene with the moderate Bader charge corresponds to the moderate adsorption energy of O atom among the MN4/graphene (M = Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe and Sc) catalysts, which results in higher activity toward Hg0 oxidation on FeN4/graphene [69]. The surface lattice constant expansion of Ru(0001) leads to the greater upshifted d-band center, which further improves CO adsorption ability, leading to Ru(0001) surface with higher activity toward CO dissociation [70]. Meanwhile, in this work, RhCo/g-C3N4 performs the highest CH2 generation activity compared with the RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts, so the relationship of d-band center and Bader charge of RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts with CH2 generation activity is considered.

The results show that CH2 formation mainly goes through the dissociation of CH2OH from the hydrogenation of CH2O or CHOH intermediates, namely, the adsorption ability of CH2OH greatly impacts CH2 generation; the adsorption energy of CH2OH at 525 K are −176.0, −172.7 and −203.1 kJ·mol−1 over the RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts, respectively; correspondingly, the RhCo cluster has the d-band center of −3.22, −2.37 and −2.98 eV; the average Bader charges of RhCo atoms are −0.49, 2.70 and 2.46 e. Namely, the moderate CH2OH adsorption ability on RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst corresponds to greater downshifted d-band center and the greater number of loss electrons, as a result, the CO bond cleavage of CH2OH easily occurs to perform high CH2 generation activity on RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst. Based on above analysis, it is concluded that the relationship of CH2 production activity with d-band center or average Bader charge shows a volcano-shaped curve.

Thus, the substrates could alter the coordination environment of RhCo active sites, and then impacts electronic properties, especially their d-band and average Bader charge of RhCo active sites to alter catalytic performance, which are also well supported by the previously reported studies. For instance, among the diatomic Fe2/graphene, Fe2/N-doped graphene, Fe2/g-C3N4 and Fe2/GDY catalysts, different substrates lead to the change of coordination environment of diatomic Fe2 active site, then, the d-band center of diatomic Fe2 active site is modulated, specifically, the moderate d-band center of Fe2/g-C3N4 catalyst presents the greater activity toward N2 conversion to ammonia [71]. Yu et al. [72] found that Ni/N, P-doped CNFs (porous carbon nanofibers) has the optimized catalytic performance of OER and HER compared with the Ni/N, S-doped CNFs, Ni/N, B-doped CNFs and Ni/N, B-doped CNFs catalysts based on the moderate d-band center induced by N, P-doped CNFs.

Once CHx monomer is generated, its related reactions easily occur, which mainly includes CHx hydrogenation to CH4, CHx reacting with CO to CHxCO, and CHx(x = 1–3) coupling [73], [74]. Our results show that CH3OH could be inhibited over RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY catalysts leading to better CHx(x = 1–3) selectivity. However, RhCo/C2N catalyst prefers CH3OH generation rather than CHx(x = 1–3), which leads to the difficult production of C2 oxygenates. Further, CH3 is the preferred CHx(x = 1–3) monomer over RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY catalysts based on the microkinetic modeling, however, CH3 generation mainly undergoes the hydrogenation of CH2, suggesting that CH2 still serves as the precursor to generate CH3. Thus, CH2 is believed to be the preferred CHx(x = 1–3) monomer, which mainly contributes to the generation of methane and C2 species over RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY catalysts.

Over RhCo/g-C3N4, see Fig. 7a, the activation free energies of CHO combined with CH2 to CH2CHO, CO combined with CH2 to CH2CO, CH2 coupling to C2H4, CH2 dissociation to CH and CH2 hydrogenation to CH3 are 136.0, 83.6, 173.0, 136.7 and 89.9 kJ·mol−1, respectively. Namely, CH2 hydrogenation to CH3 and CO combined with CH2 to CH2CO are the preferred path in the reactions related to CH2 species (89.9 vs 83.6 kJ·mol−1), as a result, the related reactions of CH3 need to be further considered (see Table 1), the activation free energies of CHO combined with CH3 to CH3CHO, CO combined with CH3 to CH3CO, CH3 coupling to C2H6 and CH3 hydrogenation to CH4 are 235.3, 85.5, 244.4 and 192.4 kJ·mol−1, respectively, suggesting that CO combined with CH3 to CH3CO is the most preferred. Moreover, the overall barriers of CH2CO and CH3CO generation beginning with CH2 monomer are 83.6 and 89.9 kJ·mol−1, respectively, so RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst dominantly contributes to the generation of C2 oxygenates CH2CO and CH3CO.

As mentioned above, the by-products such as CH4 generated by CHx hydrogenation and C2 hydrocarbons generated by CHx coupling lead to the reduced C2 oxygenates selectivity. Moreover, the overall barrier difference of the target product minus by-product has been proven to be a good descriptor for evaluating the target product selectivity, in which the negative value means the easier generation and high selectivity of target product [75], [76], [77], [78]. For example, DFT calculations by Zhang et al. [75] used the overall barrier difference between C2 oxygenates (CH2CHO) and primary by-product to analyze C2 oxygenates selectivity over the CHx(x = 1–3)/RhCu(1 1 1) surfaces in syngas conversion, the results show that CH3/RhCu(1 1 1) with the larger overall barrier difference exhibits better C2 oxygenates selectivity. Similarly, the selectivity of C2 oxygenates is quantitatively obtained by the barrier difference between C2 oxygenates and primary by-product over the five different Cu surfaces [76]. Over RhCo/g-C3N4, the overall barrier difference between CH2CO and CH4 generation is −71.5 kJ·mol−1; that between CH3CO and CH4 generation is −65.2 kJ·mol−1; namely, the generation of CH2CO and CH3CO is much easier than CH4 generation, RhCo/g-C3N4 exhibits high CH2CO and CH3CO selectivity. The overall barrier difference between CH2CO and C2H4 (C2H6) generation is −89.4 (−123.5) kJ·mol−1; the overall barrier difference between CH3CO and C2H4 (C2H6) generation is −83.1 (−117.2) kJ·mol−1, namely, the generation of CH2CO and CH3CO is much easier than C2H4 and C2H6 generation. Thus, RhCo/g-C3N4 performs high selectivity of C2 oxygenates CH2CO and CH3CO instead of CH4 and C2 hydrocarbons.

Over RhCo/GDY, see Fig. 7b, the activation free energies of CHO combined with CH2 to CH2CHO, CO combined with CH2 to CH2CO, CH2 coupling to C2H4, CH2 dissociation to CH and CH2 hydrogenation to CH3 are 229.2, 149.7, 197.5, 255.7 and 142.0 kJ·mol−1, respectively. It is concluded that the hydrogenation of CH2 to CH3 and CO combined with CH2 to CH2CO are the preferred path of CH2 related reaction (142.0 vs 149.7 kJ·mol−1), further, the related reactions of CH3 need to be examined. As shown in Table 1, the activation free energies of CHO combined with CH3 to CH3CHO, CO combined with CH3 to CH3CO, CH3 coupling to C2H6 and CH3 hydrogenation to CH4 are 116.3, 211.7, 263.3 and 104.1 kJ·mol−1, respectively, indicating that CH3 prefers to be hydrogenated to CH4. Moreover, the overall barriers of CH2CO and CH4 generation beginning with CH2 monomer are 149.7 and 142.0 kJ·mol−1, respectively. Thus, RhCo/GDY catalyst performs high CH4 selectivity instead of CH2CO.

Based on above analysis, the overall barriers of C2 oxygenate CH2CO and CH3CO generation from CH2 monomer over RhCo/g-C3N4 is much lower than that of C2 oxygenate CH2CO and CH4 generation over RhCo/GDY (83.6/89.9 vs 149.7/142.0 kJ·mol−1), namely, RhCo/g-C3N4 performs higher activity toward C2 oxygenate generation. Further, for the generation of CHx monomer and C2 oxygenates, taking the selectivity and activity into consideration, among three diatomic RhCo catalysts, RhCo/g-C3N4 is identified as the promising catalyst for the transformation of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates.

As syngas transformation to C2 oxygenates over Rh-based catalysts is usually conducted at the temperature range from 500 K to 623 K [54], [55], a reaction temperature of 525 K is mainly considered in this study, AIMD simulation is performed to estimate the thermal stability of RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst at 525 K for 10 ps with a time step of 1 fs. Meanwhile, the previously extensive studies have also used the similar duration to examine the thermal stability of g-C3N4 supported single or diatomic catalysts during AIMD simulations [79], [80], [81]. For example, Ling et al. [79] evaluated the thermal stability of B/g-C3N4 via performing AIMD simulations at 600 K for 10 ps with a time step of 2 fs, suggesting that B/g-C3N4 can maintain its structural stability at 600 K. AIMD simulations were carried out to confirm the thermal stability of Fe/g-C3N4 and Fe2/g-C3N4, in which the Fe/g-C3N4 and Fe2/g-C3N4 catalysts are very stable at 500 K without the significant migration for 10 ps [80]. The thermal stability of TM/g-C3N4 (TM = Co, Ni, Cu, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, Ir, Pt, and Au) with N vacancy was also verified via performing AIMD simulations at 500 K for 10 ps [81]. These reported studies showed that the simulation duration of 10 ps in AIMD simulations should be reliable to confirm the thermal stability of RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst.

As presented in Fig. 8, the energy and temperature oscillate around the equilibrium state in AIMD simulation process; the diatomic RhCo cluster is closely combined with the N atoms of g-C3N4 substrate, moreover, the structural deformation of catalyst occurs slightly. Thus, it is proved that the good thermal stability of RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst is presented at 525 K, which is also supported by the previous studies, for example, Fe/g-C3N4 catalyst was prepared using the method of ultrasonic-impregnation, which performs the excellent thermal stability during FTS reaction [82]. Pd/g-C3N4 catalyst could be successfully prepared by the thermally induced self-condensation to present the high stability during the process of hydrogenation of 1-hexyne [83].

On the other hand, the carbon-based substrate supported diatomic metal catalysts have been synthesized in experiment. For example, the mesoporous carbon nitride (g-C3N4) supported diatomic Pt2 catalyst were synthesized by wet chemical method to exhibit excellent catalytic performance for selective hydrogenation of nitrobenzene to aniline (the conversion rate was as high as 99 %) [84]. The diatomic FeNi/N-doped graphene catalyst was prepared using the impregnation method [85]. Pt2/graphene catalyst was successfully synthetized by the method of atomic layer deposition, specifically, the first is that Pt1/graphene catalyst is prepared at 250 °C via exposing MeCpPtMe3 and O2 over graphene surface; the second is that MeCpPtMe3 is adsorbed over Pt1 atom to obtain Pt2/graphene catalyst at 150 °C [86]. CoCu/N-doped graphene catalyst was experimentally prepared via the mixture of cobalt (II) acetate tetrahydrate, sucrose, copper(II) acetate monohydrate and urea followed by calcination at 700 °C for 2 h under Ar atmosphere, which could maintain excellent stability in syngas conversion to higher alcohol at 534 K [87]. Thus, guided by above theoretical findings and reported experimental studies, the synthesis of RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst could be realized to apply to syngas transformation process to C2 oxygenates and presents the better activity, selectivity, and the stability.

This work is performed aiming at illustrating the essential role of coordination environment in regulating catalyst stability, catalytic activity, and selectivity during the transformation process of syngas-to-C2 oxygenates. Three types of coordination environment in the carbon-based substrate supported diatomic RhCo catalysts (RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N) are considered. Here, the methods of DFT calculations combining with microkinetic modeling and AIMD simulations are adopted. The results show that RhCo/g-C3N4, RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N catalysts have excellent structural stability. Microkinetic modeling showed that RhCo/g-C3N4 exhibits higher generation rate of the preferred CHx(x = 1–3) monomer compared to RhCo/GDY and RhCo/C2N, moreover, RhCo/g-C3N4 and RhCo/GDY could effectively inhibit methanol and increase CHx(x = 1–3) monomer selectivity, subsequently, C2 oxygenates is generated through CO reacting with CHx(x = 1–3). Furthermore, the diatomic RhCo catalysts with the greater number of loss electrons and the downshifted d-band center are the essential reason to perform excellent catalytic performance for CH2 generation by electronic properties analysis. Especially, among three diatomic RhCo catalysts, the screened RhCo/g-C3N4 catalyst is the better choice for converting syngas to generate C2 oxygenates. The present study not only illustrates the essential role of coordination environment in regulating catalytic performance for syngas transformation to generate C2 oxygenates, but also offer a means to design high-performance catalysts via altering the local coordination environment of diatomic metal active site.
